opus-5.5.text:
I think I was really lucky. Back then I didn't fully understand what the ACM class was. I just knew it was a special program for students who liked computer science and wanted to go deeper. Looking back, it was one of the most important turning points in my life.

What made it special was the environment more than any single course. You were surrounded by classmates who were very passionate and very capable, and that pushes you naturally. You see people around you building things and solving hard problems, and you think, "Okay, I should try that too." The program also encouraged us to get into research quite early, which was not that common for undergraduates in China then. That's how I first came into contact with machine learning, and it planted the seed for a lot of what I did later.

The teachers also gave us a lot of freedom and trust. They would say, "Here's an interesting problem, go explore it," instead of only giving us exams to pass. I think that taught me something important: you learn the most when you're actually building and trying things yourself, even when you fail.

So for me it wasn't only an opportunity to get a good education. It shaped how I think about learning and research, and it gave me a group of friends and peers I'm still connected to today. I feel very grateful for it.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses the ACM class environment and its impact, but does not mention Professor Yu Yong remembering Chen or the care he took with his application materials.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, getting into the ACM class was honestly a bit of luck layered on top of a lot of curiosity. I'd been doing programming competitions in high school, and that gave me a route into Shanghai Jiao Tong, but the ACM class itself was something special that Professor Yu Yong had built. It was a very small cohort, very intense, and the whole idea was to take people who were good at algorithms and push them toward real research early.

What I value most about it wasn't the coursework, although that was demanding. It was the environment. You were surrounded by people who were just as obsessed as you were, and the faculty treated undergraduates as though they could actually contribute. By my second or third year I was already working in the APEX lab with Yu Yong's group, and that's where I first got exposed to machine learning, recommender systems, and large-scale data problems. That early hands-on research exposure is something most undergraduates never get.

So I see it as the place where I figured out what I actually wanted to do. Coming in, I thought of myself as a competitive programmer. Leaving, I thought of myself as someone who wanted to build systems that make machine learning work at scale. A lot of the things I did later, XGBoost, MXNet, TVM, trace back to habits I formed there: care about efficiency, care about the whole system rather than just the algorithm, and don't be afraid to build things yourself. It was a real opportunity, and I was fortunate to have people around me who pushed me to take advantage of it.

r001.rationale: The response says Professor Yu Yong built the ACM class, but does not say he remembered Chen for preparing his application materials more carefully than other students.
